name: Yara Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I push dirt for a living. I drive a dozer on the waste dumps at a big lithium mine, shaping the piles after the trucks tip, keeping the edges safe. I'm eighteen months in, after twelve years running a little bakery with my sister that didn't survive the rent rises.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst part of the day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Best part is sunrise from the top of the dump, honestly, it's beautiful in a weird moonscape way. Worst part is I'm still slow at finishing a batter slope cleanly, and the trainer, Joel, has to come and fix my edges. I use an AI app on my phone at lunch to quiz myself on the operating rules, which the old guys think is hilarious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Okay, a let-down version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, but don't let the companies use the hype as an excuse anyway. They'll still squeeze rosters and say it's for efficiency. I'd probably post something like, the robots didn't come, so where's our pay rise?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, honestly, it's a slightly boring relief. I'd keep getting better at the dozer and eventually go for the excavator ticket. I'd keep using AI for small stuff because it saves me time, hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the dozer, book my excavator ticket for next year, and keep using the AI app to study. We'd keep building the savings, we're at about two months now, and aim for four. I'd also keep going to union meetings because they're how we got the night shift allowance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, because I'm curious what's next and this is just more of the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools every day. In this world, what would you use them for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Study, mostly, plus helping Asha with her essays without writing them for her. I asked it last week to explain why our tyre pressure checks are different in hot weather and it was better than the manual. Small things, but they add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything you'd miss if AI turned out to be hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd miss the idea that it could take the boring, dangerous bits off us. There are days on the dump in the heat when I'd happily let a machine do it. Hype or not, safety's where I want it.

S0.say: I'd say don't let companies use the hype as an excuse to squeeze rosters anyway. I'd post something asking where our pay rise is if the robots didn't come.
S0.think: I think it's a slightly boring relief; I'd keep improving on the dozer and go for the excavator ticket. I'd keep using AI for small things because it saves time regardless.
S0.do: Stays on the dozer, books her excavator ticket for next year and keeps studying with an AI app. Builds savings from two months toward four and keeps attending union meetings.
S0.feel: Calm, a little flat, because she's curious about what comes next.
S0.quote: The robots didn't come, so where's our pay rise?
S0.fieldNote: Yara is the rare miner who'd be slightly disappointed by a plateau, because she likes tools that take away dull or dangerous work. Her progressive politics show in her focus on pay and rosters. She already uses AI for study and her daughter's homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels closest to what's already happening at our site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to make sure the gains get shared. If machines do more, workers should get shorter weeks or better pay, not just fewer jobs. I'd be pushing that in the union and on the community page for our town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine, maybe better off. The mine already has driverless trucks on one pit and they need people in the control room. I'm one of the few on my crew who'd actually want to sit there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my name down for the autonomous fleet control course the first time it's offered, and I'd teach myself the basics before then using online videos and AI. I'd ask Joel to mentor me on the dozer anyway, because control room people who understand the dirt are worth more. I'd keep saving, but I wouldn't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit guilty about being excited when some of my crew are scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bill, who's been on the dozers for twenty-six years and won't touch a smartphone. He taught me how to read the ground. I'd want the union to make sure people like him get a soft landing, not a pat on the back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you feel guilty. What would you do with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Use it, I suppose. Help the older guys with the paperwork for retraining, sit with them at lunch and show them the apps. My sister says I can't leave anyone behind, and she's right.

S1.say: I'd say this is the time to share the gains: shorter weeks or better pay, not just fewer jobs. I'd push that in the union and on our town's community page.
S1.think: I think I'd be fine, maybe better off, because the mine already needs control room operators for its driverless trucks. I'm one of the few on my crew who'd want that seat.
S1.do: Signs up for the first autonomous fleet control course offered and teaches herself the basics with videos and AI beforehand. Asks her trainer to keep mentoring her on the dozer, and helps older colleagues with retraining paperwork.
S1.feel: Mostly excited, with some guilt about feeling that way when others are scared.
S1.quote: Control room people who understand the dirt are worth more.
S1.fieldNote: Yara sees steady change as her opening, and she's specific about the control room path. Her guilt toward older colleagues turns into practical help. She wants gains shared through pay and shorter weeks, not only training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Oh. Two years is very fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need public ownership of some of this, or at least a big tax on it paid back to people. If AI can do all the work, the money has to go somewhere other than five companies. I'd be at rallies and I'd be loud online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared for the first time. My whole plan is the control room, and full AGI runs the control room too. Being adaptable doesn't help if there's nothing left to adapt to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still learn everything I can about the new systems in the first months, because the last humans to leave will be the ones who understand them. We'd cut back, stop eating out and pause the kids' music lessons, and get the savings to four months fast. And I'd join every campaign for a basic income, because I think that's where this ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My head's still working, but my stomach isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning change, for you specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means I can't get far enough ahead. I'd learn fast, but the machines would learn faster. With the bakery I at least saw the rent rises coming for three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Asha and Rohan that their mum is good at learning new things and we'll figure it out together. Dev would back me up, he's a teacher, he's calm with them. Privately I'd probably cry in the car park.

S2.say: I'd say we need public ownership or a big tax on AI paid back to people, because the money can't all go to five companies. I'd be at rallies and loud online.
S2.think: I think I'd be scared for the first time, because full AGI runs the control room too. Being adaptable doesn't help if there's nothing left to adapt to.
S2.do: Keeps learning the new systems so she's among the last humans needed, while cutting meals out and music lessons to reach four months of savings fast. Joins campaigns for a basic income.
S2.feel: Anxious: her head keeps working but her stomach doesn't.
S2.quote: Being adaptable doesn't help if there's nothing left to adapt to.
S2.fieldNote: The fast AGI picture is the first one that breaks Yara's confidence, because it cuts away her control room plan. She still reaches for learning, but now as a way to last longer rather than to get ahead. She ties her politics directly to who owns the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's a bit of breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to set up a proper safety net and a fair share of the gains. Start a public fund from mining profits now, so by 2031 there's something to share. That's what I'd push at the union and in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years gives me time to get into the control room and earn well for a few years. That builds savings and gets the kids closer to finishing school. It's not forever, but it's a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do the fleet control course and ask to train others on it, because trainers stay longer. I'd put any extra money from the control room into paying off the car and saving. I'd also start looking at work where people still want a person, like teaching heavy machine safety at the TAFE.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I'd have a plan, which makes it feel lighter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said trainers stay longer. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because at the bakery, when we got the new ovens, the rep who showed us how to use them had a job for years after the ovens were everywhere. Someone always has to explain the new thing to nervous people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut, if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The camping trailer we were going to buy for next summer. Dev would be sad, he's been planning trips on maps for months. But a trailer can wait, the mortgage can't.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to set up a proper safety net and share the gains. A public fund from mining profits should start now.
S3.think: I think five years lets me get into the control room and earn well for a while, building savings while the kids get closer to finishing school. It's a bridge, not forever.
S3.do: Does the fleet control course in the first year and asks to train others on it. Pays off the car, saves the extra pay, and looks into teaching heavy machine safety at the local technical college.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but lighter for having a plan.
S3.quote: Someone always has to explain the new thing to nervous people.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Yara plans a bridge rather than a destination. Her bakery story about the oven rep gives her a theory of which jobs last. She's ready to give up the family's planned camping trailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I could do a lot with ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to rebuild how work and pay are shared, so let's do it now. Shorter weeks, retraining, a fund for mining towns. I'd volunteer for the union's working group on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be okay. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be grown, and I'd have had ten years to move sideways a few times. I've already done a bakery to a lithium mine, so I know I can do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the control room course, then a training certificate, and I'd keep an eye out for jobs supervising or checking the machines. I'd keep using AI every day, it's how I learn. We'd put a bit into the super each month extra, so we're not relying on luck at sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Curious, a bit excited, and just aware it's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still keep you up at night with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether my kids get to have jobs they like. Asha wants to be a vet. I don't know what a vet looks like in 2036 and nobody else does either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the people who run the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bring us in early. Let the operators help design how it works. We know where the ground is soft and where the machines get stuck.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough to rebuild how work and pay are shared: shorter weeks, retraining and a fund for mining towns. I'd volunteer for the union's working group.
S4.think: I think I'd be okay at fifty-three with the kids grown and ten years to move sideways a few times. I've already gone from a bakery to a lithium mine.
S4.do: Moves through control room work and a training certificate and keeps an eye out for machine supervision roles. Uses AI daily for learning and adds a bit extra to retirement savings each month.
S4.feel: Calm, curious and a little excited, aware that it's coming.
S4.quote: We know where the ground is soft and where the machines get stuck.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Yara's adaptability take over again; her past career change is her proof that she can do it. Her remaining worry shifts to her daughter's future. She wants operators involved in designing the systems.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is a basic income or something like it, paid for by the companies making the money, plus free training that isn't just an online module. Give people time and dignity while they work out what's next.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could've asked what we'd actually like the robots to do. I'd give them the heat and the dust and the dangerous edges tomorrow. I just want to still have a reason to get up at five.

headlineQuote: I just want to still have a reason to get up at five.
portrait: Yara Gupta is 43, drives a dozer on the waste dumps at a lithium mine and came to mining 18 months ago after her family bakery closed. She's progressive, a union member and an everyday AI user who studies her tickets on her phone at lunch. She's calm through the plateau and Steady Disruption, seeing a path into the driverless truck control room. AGI in two years shakes her for the first time because it erases that path; with five or ten years she plans bridges and believes in her own ability to move.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because it would wipe out her control room plan before she could get ahead.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income or similar paid for by the companies profiting, plus free, real training that gives people time and dignity.
